summary: Tower built around 1960 in Woodridge Provincial Park, Manitoba; removed on 12 November 2025 over climbing concerns, without public notice.

facts.design: Tower with a ladder running to the top, behind a door
facts.status_note: Removed on 12 November 2025. The site was part of Woodridge Provincial Park, and Manitoba Parks still owns the parcel.

access.note: The former site was part of Woodridge Provincial Park. No tower remains to climb.

facts.agency: Manitoba Parks (land owner); originally Manitoba Conservation

events.note: Carillon says the tower was first built around 1960. Approximate year.
Carillon says the tower has not operated since 2010. Steinbach says it had not been used for wildfire detection in many years.
Removed on 12 November 2025. MHS describes it as demolished that day.

evidence.supports: Site was part of Woodridge Provincial Park; Prociw says it is still used for snowmobile staging, picnics and geocaching
evidence.quote: The space where the tower stood was part of Woodridge Provincial Park, and it’s still used as a snowmobile staging area, picnic spot and geocache zone, he said.

evidence.supports: Location in the Rural Municipality of Piney
evidence.quote: with residents in the Rural Municipality of Piney disappointed in losing the local landmark it became.

evidence.supports: First built around 1960; not operated since 2010
evidence.quote: It was first built around 1960 and hasn’t operated since 2010.

evidence.supports: A door covered the ladder running to the top
evidence.quote: He said he’s seen people climbing the tower, removing the door to expose the ladder running to the top.

evidence.supports: Tower and land first under Manitoba Conservation, later Manitoba Parks
evidence.quote: He explained that the tower and the land beneath it were originally under Manitoba Conservation but later shifted to Manitoba Parks after fire towers across the province became obsolete.

evidence.supports: Locals were often trained to staff the towers
evidence.quote: Locals were often the ones trained to man the towers

evidence.supports: A nearby watcher could respond faster
evidence.quote: The time for response would be so much longer if you had to wait for somebody to travel to a tower

evidence.supports: Bruce Therrien is a Sandilands resident who manned the lookout
evidence.quote: The now 60-year-old Sandilands resident was one of many locals near Woodridge who manned its lone fire lookout tower.

evidence.supports: Therrien worked in the tower during the 1980s and early 2000s
evidence.quote: Therrien worked in the tower for multiple summers during the 1980s and early 2000s.

evidence.supports: Compass and binoculars used before satellite imaging
evidence.quote: Before the shift to modern satellite imaging and other technology, Therrien was only armed with a compass and a pair of binoculars when locating fires from the tower.

evidence.supports: View of 20 miles (about 32 km) in all directions on a clear day
evidence.quote: From the tower, he could see 20 miles in all directions on a clear day.

evidence.supports: Up to 12 hours a day when fire risk was high
evidence.quote: He would sometimes spend up to 12-hours-a-day in the tower when fire risks were high.

evidence.supports: Fires were relayed between towers and triangulated
evidence.quote: If a fire was spotted, the person in the tower would take measurements on the location and relay the information to other towers so it could be triangulated

evidence.supports: Manitoba towers first detected fires in 1913
evidence.quote: Through his research, Goldsborough found fires were first detected by Manitoba lookout towers in 1913.

evidence.supports: Roughly 66 towers built across Manitoba
evidence.quote: He said there were roughly 66 towers built across the province in total.

evidence.supports: Goldsborough is head researcher at the Manitoba Historical Society
evidence.quote: Manitoba Historical Society head researcher Gordon Goldsborough

evidence.supports: Councillor Prociw: tower not used for wildfire detection in many years
evidence.quote: the tower had not been used for wildfire detection in many years

evidence.supports: Ken Prociw is councillor for Ward 1 in the Rural Municipality of Piney
evidence.quote: Ken Prociw, councillor for Ward 1 in the Rural Municipality of Piney

evidence.supports: Demolished on 12 November 2025 (MHS)
evidence.quote: It was demolished on 12 November 2025.

evidence.supports: Province removed the tower on Nov. 12
evidence.quote: The province removed the Woodridge fire lookout tower on Nov. 12, one of the last easily accessible towers in Manitoba.

evidence.supports: Taken down over concerns about people climbing, per provincial spokesperson
evidence.quote: The unused tower was taken down due to concerns about people climbing, a provincial spokesperson said in an email.

evidence.supports: Earlier efforts to restrict access had not worked
evidence.quote: Previous efforts to restrict access to the structure have not proven to be effective,

evidence.supports: No public notice before removal (Prociw and Hora)
evidence.quote: Both Prociw and Hora say there was no public notice given before the structure came down.

evidence.supports: Safety and liability likely; neither certain of the reason
evidence.quote: While neither is certain of the exact reason, both believe safety concerns and liability issues likely played a role.

evidence.supports: Locals fought to keep the tower as a landmark
evidence.quote: In the town of Woodridge, the locals fought to keep it as a landmark.

evidence.supports: Tower was included on the Woodridge Community Hall mural
evidence.quote: The tower became a symbol for Woodridge, with it included on the Woodridge Community Hall’s mural.

evidence.supports: Sandhogs have held permits for the site since 2015
evidence.quote: Since 2015, we've been getting permits to use that as a staging area

evidence.supports: Sandhogs use the staging area to load and unload ATVs for trail riding
evidence.quote: for the ATVs to use to load and offload their machines to go use the trails

evidence.supports: Gary Hora is president of the Sandhogs
evidence.quote: Sandhogs president Gary Hora said

evidence.supports: Land owned by Manitoba Parks
evidence.quote: Hora says the property, which is owned by Manitoba Parks, is unusually small.

evidence.supports: Parcel is 1.1 acres (about 0.45 hectares), the smallest park in Manitoba
evidence.quote: It's actually 1.1 acres, the smallest park in Manitoba.

evidence.supports: Therrien hopes for a monument marking the site
evidence.quote: With the tower gone, he hopes to see a monument to mark its place and honour those who served protecting the community.

corrections.why: Steinbach says the tower and its land were first under Manitoba Conservation and later moved to Manitoba Parks. None of the sources found names Manitoba Wildfire Service for this tower.

notes_for_editor: Three news and heritage-society sources agree on the removal date (12 November 2025). The build date is only 'around 1960'. No height, original builder or design source was found. The brief's agency (Manitoba Wildfire Service) is not named for this tower in any source read; see the correction. Staffing detail rests on one former lookout's account in the Carillon. The firelookout.ca index could not be read (its table loads by script), and the Manitoba Historical Society page lists no sources. Fact-check 2026-10-20: the same Carillon article also says the towers 'were first used to detect fires in the 1930s' (not attributed to Goldsborough). That conflicts with the 1913 first-detection date he gives. The story attributes 1913 to Goldsborough and does not repeat the 1930s line. Imperial figures were converted to metric with the original in brackets.
